title: The O Antiphons
hookLine: from 17 December churches sing O Wisdom, O Root of Jesse, O Key of David, O Emmanuel

lines: O WISDOM. O ROOT OF JESSE.
O KEY OF DAVID. O EMMANUEL.
cards: O Wisdom. O Root of Jesse. O Key of David.

Each of these opens a short sung verse, and in the last days before Christmas, churches that pray the evening office sing them one at a time, a new one each night, in monasteries, cathedrals and small parishes.
Every verse begins with that one open syllable, O, and every verse ends by asking for the same thing.

teach.h: A LINE THAT FRAMES MARY'S SONG.
teach.b: An antiphon is a short line sung before and after a psalm or canticle, framing it. These ones frame Mary's song, the Magnificat, at evening prayer.

teach.h: A SHOOT FROM THE STUMP OF JESSE.
teach.b: Each calls the coming Christ by a name drawn from the old scriptures, several from the prophet Isaiah.
Root of Jesse, in the King James Bible: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots." Jesse, the book of Ruth says, was the father of David.
The family tree looks cut down to a stump, and a green shoot pushes up anyway.

teach.h: HE SHALL OPEN, AND NONE SHALL SHUT.
teach.b: Key of David is from Isaiah too: "And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open."
The antiphon asks him to bring out the prisoner who sits in darkness.
And Emmanuel comes from Isaiah, taken up by Matthew at the birth of Jesus: "and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."
And each ends with a single word: come. Come and teach us. Come and set us free.
Come and save us. That's Advent in one syllable. They belong to Catholic Vespers, and Anglicans and Lutherans who keep the evening office sing them too, some in Latin, some in English.
The familiar hymn took several and set them to one tune.

how: In churches that pray evening prayer (Vespers or Evensong), one O antiphon is sung each night in the days before Christmas, before and after the Magnificat; the hymn O come, O come, Emmanuel is sung in Advent in churches of many kinds.

games.q: you're writing one of these evening verses for the days before Christmas. you've named Christ "key of David." what do you ask him to do?
o: come and open the locked door, and bring out the prisoner.
come and judge the kings of the earth.
come and build a new temple.
games.why: the antiphon asks the one who opens and none can shut to lead out the prisoner who sits in darkness.

practice: Let the names go by slowly, Wisdom, Root of Jesse, Key of David, Emmanuel, until one catches: maybe the key, if something in your life feels locked, or the shoot from the stump, if something feels cut down.
If you pray, you can say that name with the word that ends every antiphon, O Emmanuel, come; if you don't, hold the picture and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Antiphon. A short line sung before and after a psalm, framing it, as these seven do for Mary's song in the last days before Christmas.

orig.note: Hebrew: with us, God — Isaiah 7:14, which Matthew 1:23 renders "God with us."

carryVoice: Your line: o come, emmanuel. Old prophecies, with one word underneath. See you on Christmas Eve.
